title: Resistance and I–V characteristics; Electrical power and energy; Resistivity
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL03-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL05-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL03-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; EL03-1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL03-1#N.3a, EL04-1#N.4, EL05-1#N.3, EL03-1#N.11, EL04-1#N.6a, EL05-1#N.5, EL03-1#N.14a, EL04-1#N.9, EL05-1#N.10b, EL04-1#N.10a, EL05-1#N.11a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Resistance
items.clue: How strongly a component opposes the flow of charge.

items.label: Power
items.clue: Rate of energy transfer, which can be found from I²R.

items.label: Lattice ions
items.clue: Vibrating positive particles that accelerated electrons collide with.

items.label: Heating effect
items.clue: Warming of a conductor carrying a current, as collisions pass on energy.

questions.stem: Predict first. What is the origin of the electrical resistance of a metal wire?

options.text: Free electrons collide with the vibrating lattice ions, transferring energy to them.
Some of the free electrons are absorbed by the metal atoms, so fewer leave than enter.
The electrons rub against the surface of the wire, like water flowing along a pipe.
The electrons bump into one another as they crowd through the wire.

questions.stem: A uniform copper wire is cut into two pieces of equal length. How do the resistance and the resistivity of one piece compare with those of the original wire?

options.text: Its resistance and its resistivity are both halved.
Its resistance and its resistivity are both the same.
Its resistance is the same, but its resistivity is halved.
Its resistance is halved; its resistivity is unchanged.

questions.stem: The potential difference across an ohmic resistor is increased so that the current in the resistor becomes three times as large. What is the ratio of the new power dissipated in the resistor, P₂, to the original power, P₁?

options.text: P₂/P₁ = 3
P₂/P₁ = 6
P₂/P₁ = 9
P₂/P₁ = 1

questions.explanation: The resistor is ohmic, so R is unchanged. P = I²R: tripling I multiplies P by 3² = 9.

questions.stem: A student investigates whether a length of metal wire obeys Ohm's law. At the highest currents, V/I is clearly larger than at low currents. What is the best change to the method?

options.text: Use a voltmeter with a higher resolution, so the pd readings are more precise.
Take each reading twice, once with the supply reversed, and average the results.
Extend the range to even higher currents, so that more points lie on the graph.
Keep currents small or use a water bath, so the wire's temperature is constant.

questions.explanation: Ohm's law applies at constant temperature. Small currents (or a water bath) stop the wire heating, so V/I stays constant for an ohmic wire.

questions.stem: A copper cable has length 5.0 m and diameter 1.0 mm. The resistivity of copper is 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What is the resistance of the cable?
A steady current of 0.25 A flows in a 24 Ω resistor for 2.0 minutes. How much energy is dissipated in the resistor?
questions.explanation: Power = I²R = 0.25² × 24 = 1.5 W. Energy = power × time = 1.5 W × 120 s = 180 J.

questions.stem: Three components X, Y and Z are tested. The currents at pds of 1.0 V, 2.0 V and 4.0 V are: X — 0.10 A, 0.20 A, 0.40 A; Y — 0.05 A, 0.15 A, 0.35 A; Z — 0.20 A, 0.30 A, 0.40 A. Which of the components are ohmic, and why?

options.text: X and Y: each gives a straight-line graph of I against V.
None of them: V/I should double as V doubles, and does not.
X only: V/I has the same value at every reading.
X, Y and Z: V = IR applies to every one of the readings.

questions.stem: A copper wire is connected across an ideal battery. The wire is then cooled from 60 °C to 20 °C; its length and cross-sectional area change by negligible amounts. How do the wire's resistance and the current in it change as it cools?

options.text: The resistance increases, and the current decreases.
The resistance and the current both remain the same.
The resistance decreases; the current does not vary.
The resistance decreases, and the current increases.

questions.stem: A 60 W lamp and a 100 W lamp are both designed to work on the same 230 V supply. Which lamp has the larger resistance when working normally, and why?

options.text: The 100 W lamp, as a higher power needs a larger resistance.
Both are the same, as they are designed for the same supply pd.
The 60 W lamp, as at the same pd a smaller R gives more power.
The 100 W lamp, as P = I²R and it takes the larger current.

questions.explanation: At the same pd, P = V²/R. R = 230²/60 ≈ 880 Ω for the 60 W lamp and 230²/100 ≈ 530 Ω for the 100 W lamp.

questions.stem: Wire X has resistance R and is made of a material of resistivity ρ. Wire Y is made of the same material at the same temperature, but it is half as long as X and has half the diameter of X. What are the resistance and the resistivity of wire Y?

options.text: resistance R, resistivity ρ
resistance 2R, resistivity ρ
resistance 2R, resistivity 2ρ
resistance R/8, resistivity ρ

questions.explanation: R ∝ length ÷ area: the length factor is ½ and the area factor is ¼, so R_Y = (½ ÷ ¼)R = 2R. Same material and temperature, so the same ρ.

questions.stem: A 60 W lamp and a 100 W lamp are both rated for a 230 V supply. They are connected in series across a 230 V supply. Assume each keeps its normal working resistance. Which lamp is brighter?

options.text: The 60 W lamp: it has the larger resistance, and in series both carry the same current.
The 100 W lamp: it has the higher power rating, so it gives more light.
The 100 W lamp: a smaller resistance gives more power, as P = V²/R.
Both are equally bright, as they carry the same current.

questions.explanation: R = V²/P: about 880 Ω for the 60 W lamp, 530 Ω for the 100 W lamp. Same current in series, so P = I²R is larger in the 60 W lamp (about 23 W against 14 W).
